_comment: Gauntlet fixture — synthetic, scrubbed audit state. No real client material. Loaded by app/page.tsx only when ?fixture=gauntlet is present in the URL; see gauntlet/README.md.
conceptText: A returning customer opens the app and lands on a saved-orders list. Tapping an order opens a detail view with a Reorder button. Reorder skips straight to payment using the stored card, showing a confirmation sheet with the total and a 5-second undo window before the order is placed.
taskScenario: Returning user reordering a previous purchase in under three taps.

sections.label: Nielsen's 10
sections.text:
## NIELSEN'S 10 USABILITY HEURISTICS

### 1. Visibility of System Status

[PASS] The saved-orders list clearly marks which order was most recent, and the Reorder confirmation sheet shows a live countdown during the undo window.

### 2. Match Between System and the Real World

[MINOR] "Reorder" implies an exact repeat of the prior purchase, but quantities are not shown on the confirmation sheet. A returning user who changed their mind about quantity has no cue to check.

> Show the line-item quantities on the confirmation sheet, not just the total.

### 3. User Control and Freedom

[PASS] The 5-second undo window gives the user a real way out of an accidental tap before the order is placed.

### 4. Consistency and Standards

[PASS] Reorder uses the same stored-card iconography as the rest of the checkout flow described in the concept.

sections.label: Cognitive Walkthrough
sections.text:
## COGNITIVE WALKTHROUGH

### Step 1 — Open saved orders

[PASS] A habitual user returning to reorder will look for a list of past purchases first; this is a well-worn pattern from the audience's other apps.

### Step 2 — Tap an order

[PASS] The detail view surfaces the Reorder action without requiring a second navigation step.

### Step 3 — Confirm and pay

[MINOR] The concept does not describe what happens if the stored card has expired. A habitual user hitting this edge case mid-flow has no described recovery path.

> Define a fallback state for an expired or declined stored card before this ships.

sections.label: State Stress Test
sections.text:
## STATE STRESS TEST (5 UI States)

### Empty

[MINOR] No empty state is described for a user with no saved orders yet. First-time reorder flows need a described empty state, not just an absence of screens.

### Loading

[PASS] The confirmation sheet's undo countdown implies a loading/committing state is already part of the design.

### Partial

[PASS] No partial-data condition applies to this concept — a single order detail view has no partial-load case.

### Error

[MINOR] No described state for a failed reorder (e.g., item out of stock). Concept mode narrows what can be assessed here; the description commits to a happy path only.

### Ideal

[PASS] The described ideal path — list, detail, reorder, undo window, confirm — is a short, low-friction sequence appropriate for a habitual audience.

sections.label: Accessibility
sections.text:
## ACCESSIBILITY AUDIT

[MINOR] Concept mode narrows this section: with no visuals, contrast, target size, and focus-ring behaviour cannot be assessed and are not scored below.

### Time-based interaction

[MINOR] A 5-second undo window is a fixed timer with no described way to extend it. A user who needs more time — including many users who rely on assistive technology — cannot get it as described.

> Either lengthen the window or make it extendable, per WCAG 2.2.1 (Timing Adjustable).

### Confirmation semantics

[PASS] A confirmation sheet before an irreversible purchase action is a sound pattern for error prevention, assuming it is announced to screen readers when it appears.

sections.label: Overall Assessment
sections.text:
## OVERALL ASSESSMENT

### Letter Grade

**Letter Grade: B**

### Top 3 Quick Wins

1. Show line-item quantities on the Reorder confirmation sheet, not just the total.
2. Define a fallback state for an expired or declined stored card.
3. Make the 5-second undo window extendable per WCAG 2.2.1.

### What's Working Well

The reorder path itself is short and well-matched to a habitual, returning audience — list, detail, reorder, undo, confirm is a low-friction sequence with a real escape hatch built in.
